Reference: de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (2020)

Model Setting

The paper asks what the two-way fixed effects (FE) regression, a regression of an outcome on group fixed effects, period fixed effects and a treatment, estimates when the treatment effect is not constant across groups and over time. A survey finds that 19 percent of the empirical articles published in the American Economic Review between 2010 and 2012 use such a regression. The main result is that, under the standard common trends assumption, the expected FE coefficient is a weighted sum of the average treatment effects (ATEs) of all treated group-period cells, with weights that sum to one but can be negative. The weights are proportional to the residual of a regression of the treatment on group and period fixed effects, so they can be computed from the treatment data alone. Negative weights arise because the FE estimator is a weighted sum of difference-in-differences (DID) comparisons in which some “control” groups are treated at both dates, so that changes in their treatment effect are differenced out. With heterogeneous effects the coefficient can then be negative although every ATE is positive. The same holds for the first-difference (FD) regression.

The paper proposes two robustness measures: the minimal standard deviation of the cell-level ATEs under which the FE coefficient and the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) could have opposite signs, and the minimal standard deviation under which the FE coefficient could have the opposite sign of every cell-level ATE. It then proposes a new estimator, DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​, which averages DIDs comparing groups whose treatment switches between consecutive periods with groups whose treatment is stable. It is unbiased for the ATE of all switching cells under common trends assumptions on both potential outcomes, with no homogeneity restriction on the effects, and it comes with a placebo test of its identifying assumption. In the newspaper data of Gentzkow, Shapiro and Sinkinson (2011), 40 percent of the FE weights are negative, the FE coefficient is −0.0011-0.0011−0.0011, the FD coefficient is 0.0026, and DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ is 0.0043. In the union data of Vella and Verbeek (1998), DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ is 0.041 and insignificant, against an FE estimate of 0.107.

A Two-Group Example

Take a staggered design with two groups and three non-stochastic periods: group 1 is treated only at period 3, and group 2 is treated at periods 2 and 3. Suppose Ng,t/Ng,t−1N_{g,t}/N_{g,t-1}Ng,t​/Ng,t−1​ does not vary across ggg (true in a balanced panel). Then the residual is the double-demeaned treatment, and the decomposition becomes:

because ε1,3=1−1/3−1+1/2=1/6\varepsilon_{1,3}=1-1/3-1+1/2=1/6ε1,3​=1−1/3−1+1/2=1/6, ε2,2=1−2/3−1/2+1/2=1/3\varepsilon_{2,2}=1-2/3-1/2+1/2=1/3ε2,2​=1−2/3−1/2+1/2=1/3 and ε2,3=1−2/3−1+1/2=−1/6\varepsilon_{2,3}=1-2/3-1+1/2=-1/6ε2,3​=1−2/3−1+1/2=−1/6. The residual of cell (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) is negative because the linear model predicts a treatment probability above one there, a classic extrapolation problem. If the effect builds over time, with E[Δ1,3]=E[Δ2,2]=1E[\Delta_{1,3}]=E[\Delta_{2,2}]=1E[Δ1,3​]=E[Δ2,2​]=1 and E[Δ2,3]=4E[\Delta_{2,3}]=4E[Δ2,3​]=4, then βfe=1/2×1+1−1/2×4=−1/2\beta_{fe}=1/2\times1+1-1/2\times4=-1/2βfe​=1/2×1+1−1/2×4=−1/2 although all three ATEs are positive; if all three equal 1, βfe=1=δTR\beta_{fe}=1=\delta^{TR}βfe​=1=δTR. The source of the negative weight is visible in the DID representation βfe=(DID1+DID2)/2\beta_{fe}=(\text{DID}_1+\text{DID}_2)/2βfe​=(DID1​+DID2​)/2 (see also Goodman-Bacon 2018):

DID1=E(Y2,2)−E(Y2,1)−(E(Y1,2)−E(Y1,1))=E[Δ2,2]DID2=E(Y1,3)−E(Y1,2)−(E(Y2,3)−E(Y2,2))=E[Δ1,3]−(E[Δ2,3]−E[Δ2,2])(13)\begin{aligned} \text{DID}_1&=E(Y_{2,2})-E(Y_{2,1})-\left(E(Y_{1,2})-E(Y_{1,1})\right)=E[\Delta_{2,2}]\\ \text{DID}_2&=E(Y_{1,3})-E(Y_{1,2})-\left(E(Y_{2,3})-E(Y_{2,2})\right)=E[\Delta_{1,3}]-\left(E[\Delta_{2,3}]-E[\Delta_{2,2}]\right) \end{aligned} \tag{13}DID1​DID2​​=E(Y2,2​)−E(Y2,1​)−(E(Y1,2​)−E(Y1,1​))=E[Δ2,2​]=E(Y1,3​)−E(Y1,2​)−(E(Y2,3​)−E(Y2,2​))=E[Δ1,3​]−(E[Δ2,3​]−E[Δ2,2​])​(13)

In the second DID the control group, group 2, is treated at both dates, so the change in its effect between periods 2 and 3 is subtracted: the two groups' outcomes may diverge either because group 1 becomes treated or because group 2's effect changes. Negative weights come from using already treated observations as controls (also noted by Borusyak and Jaravel 2017).

Which Cells Receive Negative Weights

Proposition 1. Under a balanced panel of groups and if Ng,t/Ng,t−1N_{g,t}/N_{g,t-1}Ng,t​/Ng,t−1​ does not vary across ggg for all t≥2t\geq2t≥2: for all (g,t,t′)(g,t,t')(g,t,t′) with Dg,t=Dg,t′=1D_{g,t}=D_{g,t'}=1Dg,t​=Dg,t′​=1, D.,t>D.,t′D_{.,t}>D_{.,t'}D.,t​>D.,t′​ implies wg,t<wg,t′w_{g,t}<w_{g,t'}wg,t​<wg,t′​; and for all (g,g′,t)(g,g',t)(g,g′,t) with Dg,t=Dg′,t=1D_{g,t}=D_{g',t}=1Dg,t​=Dg′,t​=1, Dg,.>Dg′,.D_{g,.}>D_{g',.}Dg,.​>Dg′,.​ implies wg,t<wg′,tw_{g,t}<w_{g',t}wg,t​<wg′,t​. The proof is immediate from the double-demeaned residual: among treated cells, wg,tw_{g,t}wg,t​ is proportional to 1−Dg,.−D.,t+D.,.1-D_{g,.}-D_{.,t}+D_{.,.}1−Dg,.​−D.,t​+D.,.​ with a common positive factor, so it falls with the share of treated groups in the period and with the share of periods in which the group is treated. Negative weights therefore go to periods in which many groups are treated and to groups treated for many periods, and they matter when effects differ along these dimensions. In staggered adoption designs, defined by Dg,t≥Dg,t−1D_{g,t}\geq D_{g,t-1}Dg,t​≥Dg,t−1​ for all ggg and t≥2t\geq2t≥2, D.,tD_{.,t}D.,t​ increases with ttt, so wg,tw_{g,t}wg,t​ decreases with ttt (the result of Borusyak and Jaravel 2017 that the last periods are most likely to be weighted negatively, obtained here without assuming that effects depend only on time since adoption), and early adopters are more likely to receive negative weights. Athey and Imbens (2018) derive a related decomposition under random assignment of adoption dates rather than common trends.

When the Fixed Effects Coefficient Equals the ATT

The FE coefficient is robust to heterogeneity, even with some negative weights, if the weights are uncorrelated with the conditional effects:

E[∑(g,t):Dg,t=1Ng,tN1(wg,t−1)(Δ~g,t−Δ~TR)]=0(21)E\left[\sum_{(g,t):D_{g,t}=1}\frac{N_{g,t}}{N_1}\left(w_{g,t}-1\right)\left(\tilde{\Delta}_{g,t}-\tilde{\Delta}^{TR}\right)\right]=0 \tag{21}E​(g,t):Dg,t​=1∑​N1​Ng,t​​(wg,t​−1)(Δ~g,t​−Δ~TR)​=0(21)

Corollary 2. Under the five assumptions and this condition, βfe=δTR\beta_{fe}=\delta^{TR}βfe​=δTR. The proof subtracts E[∑(Ng,t/N1)Δ~TR(wg,t−1)]=0E[\sum(N_{g,t}/N_1)\tilde{\Delta}^{TR}(w_{g,t}-1)]=0E[∑(Ng,t​/N1​)Δ~TR(wg,t​−1)]=0 from the conditional decomposition and uses iterated expectations. The condition is often implausible: by Proposition 1 the groups treated longest receive the lowest weights, and they may also have the largest effects. It can be probed by correlating the weights with a predictor of the treatment effect in each cell, and this check rejects in both applications. Effects that are constant across treated cells trivially satisfy it.

The new target is the ATE of switching cells:

In staggered designs, δS\delta^SδS is the average effect in the period of adoption across all groups that ever adopt. Identification adds four assumptions. Strong exogeneity and common trends for Y(1)Y(1)Y(1) are the analogues for the treated outcome: E(Yg,t(1)−Yg,t−1(1)∣Dg,1,…,Dg,T)=E(Yg,t(1)−Yg,t−1(1))E(Y_{g,t}(1)-Y_{g,t-1}(1)|D_{g,1},\dots,D_{g,T})=E(Y_{g,t}(1)-Y_{g,t-1}(1))E(Yg,t​(1)−Yg,t−1​(1)∣Dg,1​,…,Dg,T​)=E(Yg,t​(1)−Yg,t−1​(1)), and this expectation does not vary across ggg. They allow reconstructing what leavers would have experienced had they stayed treated, and they are not needed in staggered designs, where no group leaves. Because this makes treatments dependent across groups, independent groups is replaced by mean independence: with Dg=(Dg,1,…,Dg,T)\mathbf{D}_g=(D_{g,1},\dots,D_{g,T})Dg​=(Dg,1​,…,Dg,T​), E(Yg,t(0)∣D)=E(Yg,t(0)∣Dg)E(Y_{g,t}(0)|\mathbf{D})=E(Y_{g,t}(0)|\mathbf{D}_g)E(Yg,t​(0)∣D)=E(Yg,t​(0)∣Dg​) and E(Yg,t(1)∣D)=E(Yg,t(1)∣Dg)E(Y_{g,t}(1)|\mathbf{D})=E(Y_{g,t}(1)|\mathbf{D}_g)E(Yg,t​(1)∣D)=E(Yg,t​(1)∣Dg​). The same argument with the treated-outcome assumptions gives the leavers' analogue, which compares groups remaining treated with leavers, so the leavers' effect has the sign of Y(1)−Y(0)Y(1)-Y(0)Y(1)−Y(0). Summing over ttt, dividing by NSN_SNS​ and taking expectations gives δS\delta^SδS. Stable groups guarantee that whenever there are switchers, a comparison group exists, so that no switching cell is dropped. Joiners' and leavers' effects can be estimated separately by averaging only DID+,t\text{DID}_{+,t}DID+,t​ (which needs only the assumptions on Y(0)Y(0)Y(0)) or only DID−,t\text{DID}_{-,t}DID−,t​ (only those on Y(1)Y(1)Y(1)). In staggered designs DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ averages only the DID+,t\text{DID}_{+,t}DID+,t​. As GGG goes to infinity, DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ is consistent and asymptotically normal (online appendix), and consistency holds under independent groups without the stable groups assumption. Compared with the Wald-TC estimator of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2018), DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ weights the DIDs differently and requires weaker assumptions; compared with the multiperiod DID of Imai and Kim (2018), it also covers leavers and comes with established properties. There is a bias-variance trade-off: if the FE model is correctly specified, with additive group and period effects in Yg,t(0)Y_{g,t}(0)Yg,t​(0), a constant effect δ\deltaδ and homoskedastic uncorrelated errors, the Gauss-Markov theorem makes β^fe\hat{\beta}_{fe}β^​fe​ the minimum-variance linear unbiased estimator, so DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ has a larger variance, as in both applications.

Placebo Test

DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ infers switchers' counterfactual trends from stable groups, which fails if switchers follow different trends. The placebo compares the outcome change from t−2t-2t−2 to t−1t-1t−1 between groups that switch between t−1t-1t−1 and ttt and groups that do not, among groups whose treatment was stable from t−2t-2t−2 to t−1t-1t−1. It requires stable groups for the placebo: for every t≥3t\geq3t≥3, if some group has Dg,t−2=Dg,t−1=0D_{g,t-2}=D_{g,t-1}=0Dg,t−2​=Dg,t−1​=0 and Dg,t=1D_{g,t}=1Dg,t​=1, another group is untreated at all three dates, and symmetrically for leavers. Theorem 4. Under balanced panel, sharp design, strong exogeneity and common trends for both potential outcomes, mean independence and stable groups for the placebo, E[DIDMpl]=0E[\text{DID}^{\text{pl}}_{\text{M}}]=0E[DIDMpl​]=0. Between t−2t-2t−2 and t−1t-1t−1 neither set of groups changes treatment, so each placebo DID is a difference of untreated (for joiners) or treated (for leavers) outcome trends; for joiners it equals ψ0,t−1\psi_{0,t-1}ψ0,t−1​ times weights that sum to zero, and the same holds for leavers with the common trend of the treated outcome. A placebo significantly different from zero means that switchers already trended differently from their comparison groups before switching. Unlike the standard event-study pre-trend test (Autor 2003), shown to be invalid under heterogeneous effects by Abraham and Sun (2018), it compares switchers only with stable groups. Placebos two or three periods before the switch are defined analogously.

Extensions

The decomposition extends to fuzzy designs and non-binary treatments, with essentially unchanged weights. With covariates Xg,tX_{g,t}Xg,t​ in the FE regression, strong exogeneity and common trends are replaced by

E(Yg,t(0)∣Dg,Xg)−E(Yg,t−1(0)∣Dg,Xg)=(Xg,t−Xg,t−1)′γ+λt(34)E\left(Y_{g,t}(0)|\mathbf{D}_g,\mathbf{X}_g\right)-E\left(Y_{g,t-1}(0)|\mathbf{D}_g,\mathbf{X}_g\right)=\left(X_{g,t}-X_{g,t-1}\right)'\gamma+\lambda_t \tag{34}E(Yg,t​(0)∣Dg​,Xg​)−E(Yg,t−1​(0)∣Dg​,Xg​)=(Xg,t​−Xg,t−1​)′γ+λt​(34)

with Xg=(Xg,1,…,Xg,T)\mathbf{X}_g=(X_{g,1},\dots,X_{g,T})Xg​=(Xg,1​,…,Xg,T​), and the residual in the weights is replaced by εg,tX\varepsilon^X_{g,t}εg,tX​ from the regression of Dg,tD_{g,t}Dg,t​ on the fixed effects and Xg,tX_{g,t}Xg,t​. With group-specific linear trends as covariates, the right-hand side becomes γg+λt\gamma_g+\lambda_tγg​+λt​. Covariates make common trends more plausible but do not remove the need for homogeneous effects, and some weights can still be negative. DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ extends to discrete non-binary treatments by comparing groups moving from ddd to d′d'd′ with groups at ddd in both periods. The Stata packages twowayfeweights, fuzzydid and did_multiplegt implement the weights, the robustness measures, DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ and the placebos.

Survey of AER Papers

  • Prevalence: of 337 papers published in the AER in 2010-2012, 33 (9.8 percent) estimate an FE or FD regression or a close variant (5, 14 and 14 in the three years, 5.2, 12.2 and 11.2 percent of all papers). Excluding theory papers and lab experiments, the share is 19.1 percent (12.8, 23.0 and 19.2 percent by year).

  • Methods: 13 papers use the FE regression, 6 the FD regression, 6 FE or FD with several treatment variables, 3 an FE or FD 2SLS regression, and 5 other close regressions (for instance three-way fixed effects).

  • Designs: 26 papers have sharp designs and 7 fuzzy designs; fewer than 10 percent have staggered adoption, so results limited to staggered designs cover a minority of applications.

  • Applicability of DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​: 12 papers have stable groups, 14 presumably do, 5 presumably do not and 2 do not, so the stable groups condition holds in roughly 80 percent of the papers.

Application: Newspapers and Turnout

Gentzkow, Shapiro and Sinkinson (2011) regress the first difference of turnout in county ggg between presidential elections t−1t-1t−1 and ttt (1868 to 1928) on state-year fixed effects and the first difference of the number of newspapers, which is Regression 2 with state-year controls. The treatment is not binary, so the target is strictly an average causal response rather than the ATT. Standard errors are clustered by county.

  • Regression coefficients: β^fd=0.0026\hat{\beta}_{fd}=0.0026β^​fd​=0.0026 (0.0009, 15,627 observations), so one more newspaper raises turnout by 0.26 percentage points, while β^fe=−0.0011\hat{\beta}_{fe}=-0.0011β^​fe​=−0.0011 (0.0011, 16,872 observations); the two differ significantly (t-statistic 2.86).

  • FE weights: 60 percent are strictly positive and 40 percent strictly negative, and the negative weights sum to −0.53-0.53−0.53. The estimated σ‾fe\underline{\sigma}_{fe}σ​fe​ is 3×10−43\times10^{-4}3×10−4: the FE coefficient and the ATT could have opposite signs if the standard deviation of effects across treated cells were 0.0003. The estimated σ‾‾fe\underline{\underline{\sigma}}_{fe}σ​​fe​ is 7×10−47\times10^{-4}7×10−4.

  • FD weights: 54 percent are strictly positive and 46 percent strictly negative, summing to −1.43-1.43−1.43; the estimated σ‾fd\underline{\sigma}_{fd}σ​fd​ is 4×10−44\times10^{-4}4×10−4 and σ‾‾fd\underline{\underline{\sigma}}_{fd}σ​​fd​ is 6×10−46\times10^{-4}6×10−4. The FD weights are correlated with the year (−0.06-0.06−0.06, t-statistic −3.28-3.28−3.28), while the effect of newspapers may have declined late in the period as radio spread, so uncorrelatedness is doubtful.

  • DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​: stable groups exist in every pair of elections. With state-year controls and newspapers grouped into four categories (0, 1, 2 and more than 3), DIDM=0.0043\text{DID}_{\text{M}}=0.0043DIDM​=0.0043 (0.0014, 16,872 observations), 66 percent larger than β^fd\hat{\beta}_{fd}β^​fd​ (difference significant at 10 percent, t-statistic 1.77) and of the opposite sign to β^fe\hat{\beta}_{fe}β^​fe​.

  • Placebo: DIDMpl=−0.0009\text{DID}^{\text{pl}}_{\text{M}}=-0.0009DIDMpl​=−0.0009 (0.0016, 13,221 observations), small and insignificant; the placebo subsample keeps almost 80 percent of the county-election observations, and on it DIDM=0.0045\text{DID}_{\text{M}}=0.0045DIDM​=0.0045 (0.0019).

Application: Union Wage Premium

Worker fixed effects regressions find union premia such as 8.3 percent (Jakubson 1991, PSID males 1976-1980). Using the NLSY sample of young men followed from 1980 to 1987 in Vella and Verbeek (1998), union status changes that reverse within three consecutive years are treated as measurement error and removed, which discards half of the changes. Standard errors are clustered by worker.

  • Regression coefficients: β^fe=0.107\hat{\beta}_{fe}=0.107β^​fe​=0.107 (0.030, 4,360 observations) and β^fd=0.060\hat{\beta}_{fd}=0.060β^​fd​=0.060 (0.032, 3,815 observations), significantly different (t-statistic 1.91).

  • FE weights: 820 strictly positive and 196 strictly negative, but the negative weights sum to only −0.01-0.01−0.01. The estimated σ‾fe\underline{\sigma}_{fe}σ​fe​ is 0.097, a substantial but possible degree of heterogeneity. The weights are negatively correlated with schooling (−0.12-0.12−0.12, t-statistic −1.88-1.88−1.88); if the premium is lower for the more educated, β^fe\hat{\beta}_{fe}β^​fe​ overstates the ATT.

  • DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​: 0.041 (0.034, 3,815 observations), significantly different from β^fe\hat{\beta}_{fe}β^​fe​ (t-statistic 2.60) and β^fd\hat{\beta}_{fd}β^​fd​ (2.36). The joiners' effect is 0.059 (0.053) and the leavers' effect 0.021 (0.044), not significantly different (t-statistic 0.55).

  • Placebos: DIDMpl=0.094\text{DID}^{\text{pl}}_{\text{M}}=0.094DIDMpl​=0.094 (0.038, t-statistic 2.49), while the placebos two and three periods before the switch are −0.041-0.041−0.041 (0.030) and −0.004-0.004−0.004 (0.033). The one-year pre-trend comes mostly from joiners (0.119, standard error 0.051) rather than leavers (0.061, standard error 0.057), so even the small DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​ may overstate the premium, and the leavers' effect, with no evidence of a pre-trend, is close to zero. There may be no significant union wage premium.

  • de Chaisemartin, Clément and Xavier D'Haultfœuille. 2020. “Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” American Economic Review, 110(9): 2964–2996.

These are the cell averages that carry all the information the paper uses. A cell is a (group, period) pair (g,t)(g,t)(g,t) with Ng,tN_{g,t}Ng,t​ observations. Dg,tD_{g,t}Dg,t​ is the share of treated observations in the cell; under the sharp design maintained throughout, every unit of the cell has the same treatment, so Dg,t∈{0,1}D_{g,t}\in\{0,1\}Dg,t​∈{0,1}. Yg,t(0)Y_{g,t}(0)Yg,t​(0) and Yg,t(1)Y_{g,t}(1)Yg,t​(1) are the cell means of the two potential outcomes, and Yg,tY_{g,t}Yg,t​ is the cell mean of the observed outcome.

Under the sharp design the observed cell mean equals one of the two potential-outcome means:

Yg,t=Yg,t(0)+Dg,t(Yg,t(1)−Yg,t(0))=Yg,t(0)+Dg,tΔg,t,Y_{g,t}=Y_{g,t}(0)+D_{g,t}\left(Y_{g,t}(1)-Y_{g,t}(0)\right)=Y_{g,t}(0)+D_{g,t}\Delta_{g,t},Yg,t​=Yg,t​(0)+Dg,t​(Yg,t​(1)−Yg,t​(0))=Yg,t​(0)+Dg,t​Δg,t​,

where Δg,t\Delta_{g,t}Δg,t​ is the cell ATE of equation (4). This identity is the starting point of the lemma in equation (9) and of all the DID calculations.

Working with cell means is without loss for the two-way FE and FD regressions: their regressors (group dummies, period dummies, Dg,tD_{g,t}Dg,t​) are constant within a cell, so the unit-level OLS coefficients coincide with those of a cell-level regression of Yg,tY_{g,t}Yg,t​ weighted by Ng,tN_{g,t}Ng,t​. Within-cell heterogeneity therefore never affects β^fe\hat{\beta}_{fe}β^​fe​; only heterogeneity across cells matters. The cell means are random: aggregate shocks move Yg,t(0)Y_{g,t}(0)Yg,t​(0) and Yg,t(1)Y_{g,t}(1)Yg,t​(1), and treatment assignment Dg,tD_{g,t}Dg,t​ may be random too.

These are size-weighted averages of a generic cell-level variable Xg,tX_{g,t}Xg,t​: over periods within group ggg (Xg,.X_{g,.}Xg,.​), over groups within period ttt (X.,tX_{.,t}X.,t​), and over all cells (X.,.X_{.,.}X.,.​). The weights are cell sizes divided by the relevant total, Ng,.=∑tNg,tN_{g,.}=\sum_tN_{g,t}Ng,.​=∑t​Ng,t​, N.,t=∑gNg,tN_{.,t}=\sum_gN_{g,t}N.,t​=∑g​Ng,t​ and NNN, so each average is simply the unit-level mean of XXX over the corresponding set of observations.

The first line, strong exogeneity, says that the expected change in group ggg's untreated outcome between t−1t-1t−1 and ttt does not depend on the group's entire treatment path (Dg,1,…,Dg,T)(D_{g,1},\dots,D_{g,T})(Dg,1​,…,Dg,T​), past or future. It rules out, for instance, groups selecting into treatment after a negative shock to Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) (Ashenfelter's dip), and groups whose untreated trend anticipates later treatment. It is a mean-independence condition on changes, not on levels, so levels of Yg,t(0)Y_{g,t}(0)Yg,t​(0) may be arbitrarily correlated with treatment (that is absorbed by the group fixed effect).

The new target parameter: the expected average treatment effect over all units in switching cells, those (g,t)(g,t)(g,t) with t≥2t\geq2t≥2 whose treatment differs from the previous period. It includes joiners' cells (Dg,t−1=0D_{g,t-1}=0Dg,t−1​=0, Dg,t=1D_{g,t}=1Dg,t​=1), where the effect is measured in the first treated period, and leavers' cells (Dg,t−1=1D_{g,t-1}=1Dg,t−1​=1, Dg,t=0D_{g,t}=0Dg,t​=0), where it is the effect Y(1)−Y(0)Y(1)-Y(0)Y(1)−Y(0) in the first untreated period, i.e. what leavers lose by leaving. NSN_SNS​ counts the units in switching cells, so under the sharp design the expression inside the expectation equals ∑switching(Ng,t/NS)Δg,t\sum_{\text{switching}}(N_{g,t}/N_S)\Delta_{g,t}∑switching​(Ng,t​/NS​)Δg,t​.

Why this target: switching cells are those for which a clean DID exists, comparing the switcher's change with that of groups whose treatment is stable over the same two periods. Cells that stay treated have no untreated comparison at the same dates that is not itself contaminated by changing effects, which is exactly what creates negative weights in FE. δS\delta^SδS differs from the ATT δTR\delta^{TR}δTR: it excludes treated cells that were also treated at t−1t-1t−1 (and cells treated at t=1t=1t=1) and includes untreated cells of leavers. In staggered designs, it is the average instantaneous effect of adoption among groups adopting at t≥2t\geq2t≥2. If effects are homogeneous, δS=δTR=δ\delta^S=\delta^{TR}=\deltaδS=δTR=δ.

The existence-of-stable-groups assumption is the requirement N1,0,t>0⇒N0,0,t>0N_{1,0,t}>0\Rightarrow N_{0,0,t}>0N1,0,t​>0⇒N0,0,t​>0 and N0,1,t>0⇒N1,1,t>0N_{0,1,t}>0\Rightarrow N_{1,1,t}>0N0,1,t​>0⇒N1,1,t​>0, which guarantees that no switcher is dropped. The two building blocks of DIDM\text{DID}_{\text{M}}DIDM​. DID+,t\text{DID}_{+,t}DID+,t​ compares the average outcome change from t−1t-1t−1 to ttt among joiners (untreated at t−1t-1t−1, treated at ttt) with the average change among groups untreated at both dates. DID−,t\text{DID}_{-,t}DID−,t​ compares groups treated at both dates with leavers (treated at t−1t-1t−1, untreated at ttt). The order is reversed so that the result estimates the leavers' Y(1)−Y(0)Y(1)-Y(0)Y(1)−Y(0) at ttt rather than its negative: leavers' change is Yg,t(0)−Yg,t−1(1)Y_{g,t}(0)-Y_{g,t-1}(1)Yg,t​(0)−Yg,t−1​(1), stayers' change is Yg,t(1)−Yg,t−1(1)Y_{g,t}(1)-Y_{g,t-1}(1)Yg,t​(1)−Yg,t−1​(1), and under common trends for Y(1)Y(1)Y(1) the difference has expectation equal to the leavers' average Δg,t\Delta_{g,t}Δg,t​.

Averages within each set weight groups by Ng,tN_{g,t}Ng,t​. Crucially, each comparison group has the same treatment at both dates, so no change in a comparison group's treatment effect contaminates the DID: this is what removes the negative weights of FE and FD. Each DID is set to zero when either set is empty; by the stable-groups assumption this only happens when there are no switchers of that type at ttt, in which case it gets zero weight in equation (30). Identification requires no homogeneity of effects, only the parallel-trends conditions for Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) (joiners) or Y(1)Y(1)Y(1) (leavers).

With time-varying covariates Xg,tX_{g,t}Xg,t​ added to Regression 1, the identifying assumption on Y(0)Y(0)Y(0) is relaxed to a conditional, linear version of common trends. The expected change in group ggg's untreated outcome from t−1t-1t−1 to ttt, conditional on its whole treatment path Dg\mathbf{D}_gDg​ and covariate path Xg\mathbf{X}_gXg​, equals a common period effect λt\lambda_tλt​ plus a linear function of the change in covariates, (Xg,t−Xg,t−1)′γ(X_{g,t}-X_{g,t-1})'\gamma(Xg,t​−Xg,t−1​)′γ.
